Composed by the Śramaṇa Wenguī of Dazhuangyan Monastery.

Regarding "Hetuvidyā" (Logic), it is one of the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). I have humbly investigated that the names of these five branches of knowledge have been transmitted for a long time.
However, while the *Vyākaraṇa-vidyā* (Grammar) distinguishes itself through differences in terminology and prosody, it cannot be translated [into Chinese];

as for the two sciences of *Cikitsā-vidyā* (Medicine) and *Śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā* (Arts and Crafts), being mundane matters, many have not been translated. The sūtras and śāstras translated in both ancient and modern times are mostly subsumed under the *Adhyātma-vidyā* (Inner Science).
Among these, works such as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* are all included within the *Hetu-vidyā* (Logic). Yet, some who view through a narrow tube claim that the old [translations]...

If one encounters the doctrine that there is no new existence (*anabhinavotpāda*) and, failing to comprehend it upon investigation, simply dismisses it as a heterodox treatise, this is like attempting to block the Mengjin Ford by scooping up soil without realizing its magnitude.

Furthermore, the application of *adhyātma-vidyā* (inner science) is intended for those who possess faith, while the application of *hetu-vidyā* (logic) is formulated for those who slander [the Dharma].
Indeed, the ultimate principle is profound and remote; it is not something shallow.
Because consciousness perceives objects of knowledge, various views arise in competition within the profound mysteries: some slander emptiness and negate existence;
some indulge in nihilism or revel in eternalism; some reckon that phenomena arise spontaneously, while others cling to the notion that they arise from causes and conditions;

some say "I" perform actions, while others say the "coitus" (*kula*) is the cause; some say the past and future do not exist, while others say the three periods of time exist—thus, it comes to pass that...
The paths are divided into ninety-six schools, with twenty distinct variations; yet these are all said to grasp the pearl of the Shuihou and wear the jewel of the Cakravartin King.
Since the Dharma-gate is non-dual, how could there be different destinations? There is but one principle: if one is true, then the others are false.
Thus, if one wishes to observe whether forms are beautiful or ugly, one uses a clear mirror or a limpid pool to discern them, establishing the principle and rectifying it.
The heterodox must necessarily be illuminated by means of *hetuvidyā* (logic) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:

"The skillful means of the treatise on *hetuvidyā* constitutes the method for discerning phenomena. For this reason, while the Great Sage taught *hetuvidyā* diffusely, his disciples compiled it into a separate section.
Some preserved its title as "Yathārtha" (As It Truly Is), while others designated it as "Nyāya" (Right Reasoning). Therefore, Vasubandhu studied the traditional five-membered syllogism.
The bones manifest virtue; Dignāga first codified the three treatises, and his roar resounded upon the stone to manifest his capacity.

Regarding this great enterprise, it is difficult to record the pursuit of his legacy or the preservation of his fragrance. There was a Bodhisattva named Śaṅkarasvāmin, who possessed innate knowledge of the ultimate truth and was skilled at discerning the capacities of beings.
He thus condensed the extensive texts to compose this concise treatise, desiring to enable those who have newly begun their studies to recognize the general direction of the path.
Among those who have ascended these halls, there are few who understand the origins of this "Ten Chapters.

Now, the Tripitaka Master, whose capacity exceeds that of the *hu* and *lian* vessels and whose Way surpasses that of a ship or raft, sighed at the darkness of the masses and took it to heart; he resolved to perfect his studies through the Five Sciences.

He sought the Way in the Western Regions and devoted himself to these texts, returning to the Eastern Capital where he promptly began the translation. [I], being of dull wit, [have recorded] the *Gui* (the rules/track).

The phrasing of these texts is obscure and their doctrines superficial; fortunately, we have entered the same chamber together and heard the instruction as clearly as one points out the palm of one's hand.

I have recorded these matters time and again to defile the records of the great sash. What I regret is that scholars today establish doctrines that are not based on the fundamental schools and find it difficult to follow fixed rules.
They do not honor the great canon of *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), but instead admire the vulgar talk of common streets, even claiming that "the eight [categories] are all eight."
If one turns this into a pivot for the four gates, it is not a lofty discourse;

or if one studies the provisional dharmas within the initial chapters, or relies on texts such as the "Dragon Moving and Snake Coiling" (Longyou Sheshi), these all blend words and principles so thoroughly that victory and defeat cannot be distinguished.

When questions and answers arise like mountain peaks, who can determine right from wrong? One should simply regard the latter as superior in expression, rather than considering the former as superior in principle.
Those who study correctly do not realize that habitual practice gives rise to the mundane; how could it be otherwise?

By means of *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), one can comprehensively encompass all treatises, thereby serving as a balance for establishing and refuting, providing a standard for determining the correct and the false, and allowing for the praise or censure of right and wrong.
Once the sun and moon have shone clearly, the torches of fire naturally extinguish themselves; once the drenching rain has fallen, the irrigation is complete.

There is no [independent] gift. As for what is called the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* (The Treatise on Entering Right Reasoning through Causality): "Causality" (*hetu*) has the meaning of using the cause to bring about the effect;
"clarity" (*praveśa*) has the function of causing unarisen wisdom to arise so that it may illuminate; and "right reasoning" (*nyāya*) has the function of making unmanifest meanings manifest.
"Manifest" refers to the text itself, which is titled "Entering" (*praveśa*). Thus, both "entering" and "right reasoning" are names for the result.
If both "cause" (*hetu*) and "clarity" (*vidyā*) are termed "causes," they are called so because they are the immediate conditions for the arising of the fruit;

thus, the term "cause" simultaneously encompasses both the meaning of "wisdom" (*jñāna*), which directly realizes the fruit through its penetrating discernment, and the meaning of "clarity," which indirectly extends to that same realization. Since the substance of the fruit is not manifold, the term "entry into principle" (*tattvapraveśa*) refers exclusively to the meaning of wisdom.
This is the assessment of the commentators (*vibhāṣā-kārāḥ*). That is, they evaluate [the text] by means of eight topical gates (*aṣṭadvāra-vibhāga*).
Because both [the author and the title] employ words to exhaustively elucidate the principles, it is called a *śāstra* (treatise); thus, it is titled the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin":
Śaṅkara was a manifestation of Maheśvara who appeared in the world to guide sentient beings; his physical form resembled a skeleton, and he was thus named Śaṅkara.
People of that time admired him and depicted his image for reverent worship;

because the Master’s birth was in response to prayers to this deity, he consequently presided over this deity and took it as his title—thus, Śaṅkara became his primary name, and he is known as Śaṅkarasvāmin.

The means of proof (*sādhana*) and the means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), along with their fallacious counterparts (*tadābhāsa*), serve solely to instruct others; direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), along with their fallacious counterparts, serve solely for one’s own understanding.

The translation above renders the headings as a structured list and the commentary as a prose explanation.*

the first four gates combined as "realization for others" (*parāvabodha*), and the latter four gates combined as "self-realization" (*svāvabodha*). Regarding the first four gates: 1. The Prover (*sādhana*: skillfully presenting inference to uniquely manifest one's own thesis and [overcome] false adversaries).

Concealing one's words is why it is called "able to establish" (nirūpaṇa). Second, the "pseudo-establishment" (pratirūpaka): when the three members [of a syllogism] are fallacious and presented with false attachments, it is as precarious as a stack of eggs; thus it is called pseudo-establishment. Third, the "able to refute" (dūṣaṇa):

when one skillfully censures the error of the thesis, or challenges the reason and the example with a majesty like that of pursuing a defeated army; thus it is called able to refute. Fourth, the "pseudo-refutation" (pratidūṣaṇa): when one attempts to resist with the axe of a mantis while the enemy’s chariot has already descended, offering a spurious objection; thus it is called pseudo-refutation.

The two terms "pseudo" (pratirūpaka) and "like" (pratidūṣaṇa) encompass the aforementioned establishment and refutation, and thus there are four categories. Indeed, the emergence of establishment and refutation occurs within verbal discourse.

Once discourse has arisen, the deviant and the correct can be distinguished; this distinction resides in speech. While the principle is not realized through self-awakening, the presentation of proofs and refutations through speech is for the sake of others.
Although these may differ in their outward appearance, all such utterances are intended to benefit sentient beings.

Thus, these four meanings together constitute "awakening others. As for the latter four gates: first is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which realizes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena without being bound by names or concepts, like a mirror reflecting forms.

Therefore, it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Sixth, pseudo-direct perception: to gaze at the dark and yellow [colors] while claiming to see a vase and the like, or to regard a whirling firebrand as seeing it—this is called pseudo-direct perception.

Seventh, inference (*anumāna*): relying on the manifest to reach the hidden meaning, so that the categories may encompass and accord with the True Doctrine—therefore, it is called inference. Eighth, pseudo-inference: to depict a form in a shadow without exhausting its beautiful features; to imitate it and yet lose the truth—this is called pseudo-inference.
Furthermore, the two terms "pseudo" (*sadṛśa*) apply to the aforementioned direct perception and inference, which also have four gates. Now, the arising of direct perception and inference lies in...
Regarding consciousness: once consciousness arises, the deviant and the correct can be distinguished; this distinction resides within the mind and is not realized through anything else.

When the mind dwells in the present, it is sufficient to clearly manifest self-benefit. Although there may appear to be differences between the correct and the deviant, internal discernment reveals that both serve to enlighten oneself.
Therefore, these four meanings are combined as "Self-Enlightenment. [Question: One must first cure one's own illness before one can save others; for what reason is this so?

Regarding this, the preceding section [of the *Abhidharmakośa*] explains awakening others, while other sūtras are based on the sequence of the arising of practice, which necessarily proceeds from oneself first and then to others.
This treatise, however, clarifies the principles of establishing and refuting; therefore, it treats "others" first and "self" later.
Some explain this difficulty by saying that because a bodhisattva cherishes others before himself, it is not the case that awakening others is mentioned first within this treatise. Is this not so?
Is it that one must first explain impermanence to others before subsequently inferring the meaning of impermanence for oneself? Therefore, the former interpretation is correct.
In this way, the essential points of all treatises are comprehensively subsumed.

and (3) "For now, let it suffice," etc., restraining the explanation to manifest its brevity. This is the first part.

Because the ancient compositions were clearly seen to be verbose and complex in both wording and meaning, these verses were compiled to encompass the essentials completely. To manifest this superior capacity, it says "as follows."

First, the determination by way of essence; second, the establishment through function. This refers to the first [determination by way of essence].
Regarding the phrase "in this context" (*atra*), there are two meanings: first, it is a general term used when about to state something;

second, it is a selective term meaning "this" as opposed to "that," specifically selecting the *sādhana* (the means of proof) from among the eight categories. This refers to the multiple terms such as the *pakṣa* (thesis), and so forth.

Regarding what is called the "proof" (*sādhana*), the masters prior to Dignāga all maintained that the thesis (*pakṣa*) consists of one statement, the reason (*hetu*) of two statements, and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of three statements;
since a plurality of words is simply called a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*), these multiple statements are collectively termed the "proof.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The objects to be proven (*sādhya*) are twofold: first, the essential nature (*svabhāva*)."

The two distinctions regarding form (*rūpa*) and so forth refer to the "visible" and so on. There are eight [members]: first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*);

sixth, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); seventh, inference (*anumāna*); and eighth, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). Dharmakīrti states that the word "thesis" refers to that which is to be established (*sādhya*), while the "reason" and so forth are the means of establishment (*sādhana*).

By mentioning the means of establishment and so on, the intention is to include that which is to be established and so forth; thus, the "means of establishment" implies the "object to be established."
The middle reason, based on one example, consists of two parts, which together constitute the "many words.

These many words are called the *sādhana* (the means of proof), because the *sādhana* establishes that which is to be established (*sādhya*). If one does not state the *sādhya*, it would be unknown whose *sādhana* it is.
Dignāga’s intention was that the ancient masters claimed the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are all equally the *sādhana*.

Regarding that which is to be established (*sādhya*), one selects a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*) from among its various elements according to one’s own intention, and combines them to form the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Since the thesis is thus a combination of those general and specific properties, it is not distinct from their totality; therefore, it is the means of proof (*sādhana*).

Now, the intention of Dignāga is this: he originally intended to combine specific properties as the thesis, desiring to establish that thesis by means of a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Since the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is that which establishes (*sādhana*), and that which establishes must establish the thesis (*pakṣa*), we know that the thesis is that which is to be established (*sādhya*).
Thus, according to the ancient masters, because the thesis is viewed in relation to its specific properties, it is that which effects the proof;

however, Dignāga maintains that when the thesis is viewed in relation to its reason (*hetu*) and example, it is indeed that which is to be established. Question: Since there are eight types of *sādhana* in the Abhidharma, why is only [the thesis] mentioned here?

Third, the response: these three parts here subsume the five members of the Abhidharma; the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) and "reason" (*hetu*) correspond to those [members], while the "example" (*udāharaṇa*), "application" (*upanaya*), and "conclusion" (*nigamana*) subsume the example and the application-conclusion of that treatise.
Since the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of that treatise are included within this treatise’s "door of self-realization," they are not included within the "door of realization for others.
Question: Since those means of valid cognition are three, why are there only two here? Answer: The "scriptural authority" (*āptāgama*) is...
This will be explained in the text when it is subsumed under inference (*anumāna*).
Because the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) reveal the meaning to those questioners who have not yet understood it through many words.
The commentary states: this is established by way of function. For instance, regarding meanings such as impermanence (*anityatva*), if the opponent has not yet clarified their realization—namely:

Due to ignorance, one does not know that this is impermanent; due to knowledge through doubt, one wonders whether it is permanent or impermanent; and due to inverted knowledge, one claims it to be permanent.

Now, the proponent establishes the thesis by means of multiple expressions such as the *pakṣa* (thesis) and so forth, in order to reveal and cause understanding. The word "therefore" (*hi*) serves to establish the proof;
that is to say, it indicates that the function of causing the opponent to understand and realize [the truth] is achieved through the thesis and the other members of the syllogism. Thus.

Excessive speech is called "establishing a proof. If the opponent hears it once and does not understand, one should inquire further; for even if there was understanding upon first hearing, there may still be grounds for questioning.
Both the opponent and the person providing the proof are called "questioners. Now, as for the person who provides the proof, they are one who is proficient in all schools of thought (*sarvatantra*).
Why, then, is it said that they have not yet fully understood the meaning? The answer is: although the person providing the proof has long understood it, they have temporarily set it aside.

It is revealed for the sake of causing one who has forgotten to remember; furthermore, it is revealed by the proponent of the thesis because when opponents create confusion through contradictory proofs, the mind becomes distracted, and thus wisdom regarding the meaning and principle does not arise. Therefore, the proponent reveals it once again.
Regarding the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) herein, the commentary states:

what follows below is the second [section], the explanation of the essential nature (*tattva*), which has three parts: first, the thesis; second, the reason (*hetu*); and third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now, first is the explanation of the thesis, which has three parts: first, the restatement of the chapter title; second, the preliminary explanation; and third, the indication of the essence. This is the restatement of the chapter title, namely the three members (*trirūpa*).
This restates the initial thesis.
It refers to the "established subject" (*prasiddha-dharmin*) and the "established qualifier" (*prasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: from here below is the second section, the preliminary explanation, which has five parts: first, identifying the basis; second, clarifying the essence; third, demonstrating the rule; [and so forth].

The fourth [section] excludes confusion, and the fifth establishes the definition; this is the first [of those]. Regarding the statement that "there is a phenomenon (dharma) capable of differentiating":
phenomena are of two kinds. First, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such as form, sound, fragrance, and so forth. Second, differentiation (*viśeṣa*), such as permanence, impermanence, and so forth.

Intrinsic nature has two names: first, "the phenomenon" (*dharmin*); second, "that which is to be differentiated" (*viśeṣya*). Differentiation has two names: first, "the property" (*dharma*); second, "that which differentiates" (*viśeṣaka*).

The meaning of "dharma" is that which possesses the principle of being permanent, impermanent, and so forth; because form, sound, and the like possess this dharma, they are called "possessors of dharma" (*dharmī*).

Because these very things—form and so forth—are differentiated by the distinctions of permanence and impermanence, making them distinct from internal and external phenomena, they are called "the differentiated" (*viśeṣya*).
Since permanence, impermanence, and so forth can indeed differentiate the self-nature of form and the rest...

Regarding the thesis that "sound is a jar," the response is twofold: in both cases, the function (*kārya*) is established.

Since these two characteristics together serve as the reason (*hetu*), how can you claim that the thesis is established in both cases when the jar is impermanent but sound is not? How, then, can it be said that the thesis is established in both places?

Regarding the third characteristic: this also correctly apprehends the non-existence of the object to be negated (*pratiṣedhya*) while simultaneously apprehending the constant absence of the negation itself (*pratiṣedha*). Question:

Why is it that the term "only" (*eva*) is used to establish the certainty of coexistence (*sahabhāva*), yet no such statement is made regarding the pervasiveness (*vyāpti*) of the distinct non-existence?

Answer: The term "coexistence" is employed to facilitate the establishment of certainty; for if there is certainty of existence, it facilitates the establishment of the exclusion of confusion. However, in establishing the distinct non-existence, pervasiveness is not required because confusion is not excluded [by mere certainty]. Therefore, the word "coexistence" implies certainty.
"Vipakṣa" means "pervasive. Question: For what reason are only these three characteristics established? Answer: Because no other characteristics can be established.

Their first characteristic does not differ from Dignāga’s; however, their latter two characteristics both take the "subject" (*dharmin*) as their entity, such as a jar.

Since that which is "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "impermanent" (*anitya*) upon [the locus of] a jar and so forth both take the jar and so forth as their essence, the jar and so forth constitute the second characteristic.

Since that which is "eternal" (*nitya*) and "unproduced" (*akṛtaka*) upon [the locus of] space and so forth both take space and so forth as their essence, space and so forth constitute the third characteristic.
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* composed by Vasubandhu states: "There are three kinds of reasons (*hetu*), namely..."
This fundamental dharma is subsumed under its own kind and separated from those of different kinds; this treatise was translated by Paramārtha during the Liang period.

"If it were explained in this way, it would cause the reason (*hetu*) to incur the fallacies of being either non-genuine or pseudo-reasoned. Why? For example, consider the case of establishing [the existence of] space..."
This is the reason for permanence: because it is not produced. The concordant example states: "All things that are not produced are permanent, such as *nirvāṇa*.
The discordant example states: "If something is impermanent, it is produced, like a jar or a basin.
Since the impermanence of the jar directly contradicts and subverts the permanence of space, it is termed a "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*). However, the tortoise...

Since [the subject] such as hair is not non-eternal, it cannot harm that which is eternal; thus it is not a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, because it is not eternal, it is not called a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

This [reason], "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), applies to that [eternal space] as well; since it thus possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*), it cannot be said to be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

However, because it fails to exclude [the possibility of overlap] due to its lack of precision, it cannot be said to be a true [reason]. That is to say, this [proponent] takes this empty space (*ākāśa*) as the "similar instance."
Is Nirvāṇa eternal because it is unconditioned? Or is it neither eternal nor non-eternal, like a tortoise’s hair, because it is unconditioned?
If my interpretation is correct, then that which lacks a locus for the probandum (sādhya) is designated as the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Since a tortoise’s hair does not exist, the property of being eternal is likewise a dissimilar instance. Thus, this reason—"because it is unconditioned"—is [unestablished] with respect to...
Because it occurs in only one part of the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), it is a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).

Furthermore, if a permanent phenomenon is designated as the dissimilar class because it excludes impermanence, then since a tortoise’s hair cannot exclude that impermanence, it would not be the dissimilar class;

subsequently, if it were not impermanent, it could not be called the similar class (sapakṣa). If this were the case, one would have to establish a class that is neither similar nor dissimilar, and the reasons would likewise have to be established as being of four types.

The characteristics are not merely three; furthermore, another master says: "For example, if one establishes that sound is impermanent, then that which is simply different from impermanence constitutes the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
Dignāga refutes this, saying: "If explained in this way, there would be the fault of an absolute lack of a valid reason (*hetu*).
Why? For instance, when establishing that sound is impermanent, the 'selflessness' (*anātmatva*) inherent in sound is different from the thesis (*pakṣa*) of impermanence."

This refers to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Since the probans (*kṛtakatva*) exists within the dissimilar instance—namely, that which is "without self"—it becomes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
In this way, for every single property (*dharma*) that exists, its cause operates within a distinct meaning;
thus, there is ultimately no correct reason at all. According to my interpretation, that which is not the locus of the thesis (*sādhya*) is called the dissimilar instance.
Thus, although sound and other phenomena lack selfhood, because that which is to be established (the probandum) exists, the reason does not occur in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);
therefore, it attains the status of a valid reason (saddhetu).
In this context, the nature of being produced (kṛtakatva), or the nature of being produced through diligent and uninterrupted effort, [is the reason].

The commentary states: Below this, the nature [of the path] is distinguished in three parts: first, directly indicating its essential nature; second, clarifying the nature by way of its characteristics;

some say this refers to vigor (*vīrya*), while others say it refers to mental attention (*manasikāra*). As for "that which is emitted without interval," it proceeds from...
Diligent effort (*ābhoga*) gives rise to the mind; from the mind arise applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); from applied and sustained thought arises internal wind;

by means of this internal wind, [the sound] reaches as far as the lips, mouth, and so forth, thereby becoming sound. Therefore, it is said: "Alternatively, its nature is that which is produced without interval by diligent effort.

Question: Since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is a single cause, why are there two? Answer: The thesis also has two aspects. First, the broad [definition], which establishes sound as being both internal and external.
"This is impermanent" is based solely on the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) as the reason; this is twofoldly narrow.
That is to say, establishing that internal sound is impermanent takes its cause to be "that which is produced by effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*).

Although this nature of being produced is indeed a valid reason for the aforementioned thesis, because it is too broad, one takes only "being produced by effort" as the reason. This is explained in terms of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
This characteristic of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) is further explained here as being twofold, based on whether it exists pervasively or non-pervasively within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

That is to say, the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) exists pervasively among similar instances, whereas the reason "arising from volitional effort" (*prayatnāntarīyakatva*) does not exist pervasively among similar instances.

therefore, although the statement includes [the example], the members remain distinct. Although there are two types of concordant examples, they both equally assist the reason (*hetu*); thus, they are treated as a single member. This is the explanation by Vasubandhu.
The opponent states: "The two properties—the 'being produced' in a jar and the 'being produced' in sound—are combined and termed 'homogeneous' (*sādharmya*).

Dignāga refutes this, saying: "If one infers that sound is impermanent because it is produced, on the grounds that a jar is produced and is impermanent, then it would follow that a jar is visible and combustible, while sound is produced, yet is neither visible nor combustible."
If the observed property (*dṛṣṭa*) is not similar to the jar, how can it be impermanent? [The opponent asks: "In what way is it similar to sound? Dignāga explains:

"The 'produced' nature (*kṛtaka*) in sound manifests its impermanence in the same way that the 'produced' nature in a jar manifests its impermanence. Because this [sound] is similar to that [jar], it is called 'similar in dharma' (*sadharmya*).
One takes up the commonality (*sādharmya*) itself, not the object of the commonality. This interpretation is likely incorrect, for if Vasubandhu and others [were to argue] by means of the jar...
Because it is produced, it is impermanent; likewise, sound is produced and is therefore impermanent. To this, an objection is raised:
"A jar is produced, visible, and combustible; but sound, though produced, is neither visible nor combustible.

Since Dignāga has already used the fact that sound is produced to demonstrate its impermanence—just as the fact that a jar is produced demonstrates its impermanence—how can it be said that sound is produced yet invisible?
If one argues that because things produced by an external pot are seen to be combustible and impermanent,
internal sound produced by [a cause] is likewise impermanent— just as an external pot is seen to be combustible—
then since Dignāga has already used the impermanence of internal sound produced [by a cause] as a parallel for the impermanence of an external pot produced [by a cause], [the argument is redundant].

Why do you not always apply the same reasoning? Just as the visible jar that is produced by sound and is subject to burning is impermanent, so too, if you claim that the "burning-visible" is an external jar and cannot be categorized by sound, then it must also be impermanent.

Since it is an external jar, how can it be categorized by sound as being impermanent? This is the same error as the old interpretation of Dignāga; although one distinguishes between internal and external, in the end—

Furthermore, it cannot be otherwise; for in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, Dignāga states that among the treatises on the rules of debate (*vādanyāya*), those which employ a jar as the subject (*dharmin*) of the example (*sapakṣa*) were either not composed by Vasubandhu or were composed before Vasubandhu had completed his studies.
Once he had mastered them, the formal style of the treatises took the "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) as the body of the example.

Since this very point—that it is not different from my own position—is already stated in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, how can you claim that Vasubandhu incurs the fault of [illegitimately] applying the properties of a jar’s being produced and impermanent to internal sound, thereby resulting in the faults such as "being combustible"?

My current explanation is that the faults such as "being combustible" merely refute the formal logic of the treatise; for instance, when one takes a jar as the property-possessor (*dharmin*) to serve as a similar example (*sapakṣa*), these [faults] apply.
