This very essence of the jar serves as the homogeneous example (dṛṣṭānta). This master formulates the syllogism (*prayoga*) as follows:
"Sound is impermanent; because it is produced; like a jar. That is to say, "like a jar, which is impermanent. Dignāga refutes this, saying: "If one uses the jar directly..."
If one were to employ a "homogeneous example" (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) by classifying sound as impermanent because the substance of a jar is impermanent,

then it would also follow that the jar— being composed of the four sense-objects (*catuḥ-viṣaya*) and being visible and combustible— would likewise have sound, which is also composed of the four sense-objects and is visible and combustible. If, according to my interpretation,

the nature of all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) is taken as the body of the example because they are all impermanent, then jars and the like are not the examples themselves, but rather the substrata (*āśraya*) upon which the example is based.
Thus, there is no such fault. If one asks: "Since a jar is produced (*kṛtaka*), it is impermanent;
likewise, since sound is produced, it too is impermanent"—then it would follow that a jar, being produced, is combustible and visible, while sound, being produced, is also combustible and visible.

This would mean the fault is identical [to yours]. Why does the ancient master Dignāga refute this by taking only "being produced" as the reason? [The answer is: Dignāga merely takes "being produced" [as the probans].
Taking impermanence as the illustrative essence (*dṛṣṭānta-dravya*), one does not take the four sense-objects (*catuḥ-spraṣṭavya*) [as the essence].
It cannot be objected that sound belongs to the same category as a jar and so forth, being visible and combustible;

for if one were to forcefully raise such an objection outside of the illustrative essence, it would contradict the ancient masters themselves, who already took jars and the like as the illustrative essence, since a jar possesses the four sense-objects and is both combustible and visible. Thus, [the objection] is untenable.
The objection states: "If a jar can be burned and seen, then sound should likewise be so. Question: "If you raise this objection, does it not contradict your own position? Answer:

"In the method of analogical illustration, the phenomenon must necessarily resemble the example. Since the ancient masters have already used a jar as an analogy for sound, it follows logically that the ancient masters themselves would have to admit that [sound] can be burned and seen.
To claim otherwise—that it cannot be seen—is merely a forced objection attempting to equate it with a jar."

Therefore, raising this objection does not entail the fault of self-contradiction. [Objection: Since the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (The Compendium of Reality) clarifies that the reason has three characteristics (*trirūpa*), why is the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) not identical to the second characteristic?
[Response: That second characteristic is manifested through the member of "application" (*upanaya*).

It is stated: "A jar is produced; a jar is impermanent. One should know that sound, being produced, is likewise impermanent. Thus, it is by means of the application that the second characteristic is made explicit.

Therefore, regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*), we have taken only the jar and so forth; other refutations are omitted here for the sake of brevity, as they are explained at length in the *Nyāyamukha*.
As for the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*):

The commentary states: This explanation concerns the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) and has two parts: first, the citation of the section; second, the explanation. This is the citation of the section:
"If, in a certain case, it is stated that the probandum (*sādhyadharma*) is absent and the reason (*hetu*) is entirely non-existent."
The commentary states: Below this, the explanation has three parts: first, a preliminary interpretation; second, pointing to the essence;

and third, resolving difficulties. This is the first [part]. "Locus" (*dharmin*) refers to the subject of the proposition; "non-existent" (*asat*) refers to the non-existence of the property to be established (*sādhya-dharma*).
"Because the reason is entirely non-existent" means that the probative reason (*hetu-dharma*) is entirely non-existent. This, then, correctly takes up that which is non-existent.
The "dissimilar example" (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is so named because it simultaneously lacks the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and the probandum (sādhyadharma).
If it were defined merely by the absence of the property of the subject, then that which is not present in the similar class (sapakṣa) would have to be considered a dissimilar example.
That is to say: "If it were eternal, it would not be something produced.

[The commentary] states: "The following refers to the essential nature (*tattva*). First, the essential nature is directly indicated; subsequently, its basis is cited. This is the first [part]. That is to say:
"If it were eternal," refers to the non-existence of that which was previously established as the thesis (*sādhya*); "seen to be not something produced" refers to the previous...
The cause is not omnipresent, like space and so forth. [Commentary:

This cites the basis [of the analogy]. The phrase "and so forth" includes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and that which is commonly accepted.
To take all these as equal, they are immediately resolved within the context of this point. The meaning of this analogy is as follows:

just as in space there is nothing established above it, there would be no probandum (*sādhya*)—the thesis of impermanence—if there were no probans (*sādhana*), namely the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), upon the sound.
Since the reason of "being produced" exists upon the sound, one knows for certain that there must be the probandum of impermanence.
In this context, the term "permanent" (nitya) indicates that which is not impermanent, and the term "uncreated" (akṛtaka) indicates that which is not produced.
[The author] states: "This is a general response to the objection. First, he provides the correct response to the objection; second, he cites an example to prove it.

This is the first part. Here, there should be an objection: "Since space is established as being omnipresent and can be spoken of, according to the school that asserts the existence of space, its essence (svabhāva) must likewise exist."

Because there is neither a corresponding nor a dissimilar example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is now explained comprehensively as follows: here, the term "permanent" merely indicates that which is not impermanent;
it does not intend to define "permanent" as being non-produced (*akṛtaka*). Likewise, the term "non-produced" merely indicates that which is not produced;
it does not intend to define "non-produced" as being non-existent. Therefore, even when debating with those who do not posit space (*ākāśa*), one may still take space as a dissimilar example.
Because the emptiness of non-substantiality also negates impermanence, it is termed "permanent. Since it negates that which is produced, it is said to be "unproduced";
thus, even a tortoise's hair can be described as permanent and unproduced.
"If that which exists is not [ultimately] existent, it is called 'non-existent.

The commentary states: This is an introduction of an example as proof. Here, the categories of the Vaiśeṣika school are cited as an illustration; the Vaiśeṣika system posits six categories (*padārtha*):

first, substance (*dravya*); second, quality (*guṇa*); third, action (*karman*); fourth, existence (*sattā*); fifth, particularity (*viśeṣa*); and sixth, inherence (*samavāya*). What is here referred to as "existence" (*sat*) is—

Regarding "the fourth is existence and non-existence": this refers to the remaining five propositions as well as those phenomena not subsumed within the five propositions, such as the hair of a tortoise, which are designated as "non-existent.
This is called "non-existence" because it negates the proposition of "existence" by being the non-existence relative to existence;
however, the term "non-existence" does not necessarily imply that there is a substantial essence of non-existence. Now, it is said:
The terms "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth are also explained in the same way. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "existent" (*bhava*) refers to the category of existence;

"non-existent" (*abhava*) does not refer to the fourth realm of existence (*bhava*). It is called "non-existent" because it is not the category of the fourth existence; thus it is termed "non-existent.
Regarding the statement that "eternal" and so forth do not establish the essence of the category of non-existence, this means they do not express permanence or non-existence.

[Question: Regarding the nature of the subject, why does the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) merely express negation without separately designating the existence of an entity, whereas the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) designates the existence of an entity?

Should this [dissimilar example] not also negate [the existence of an entity]? [Answer: All phenomena possess two characteristics: first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and second, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

For instance, the specific characteristic of blue is apprehended solely by visual consciousness; however, the general characteristic of "blue" is known by mental consciousness. Names and words (*nāma-pada*) designate only [the latter].
The universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of blue does not express its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the particular characteristic of blue is beyond verbal expression.
To express the universal characteristic of blue, one must exclude yellow and other colors; that is, by negating "non-blue," it is designated as "blue.
If one did not exclude non-blue while calling it "blue," it would follow that yellow and other colors would also be called "blue. Therefore, all names intend to apprehend their respective phenomena.

One must negate other means of expression for this [non-existence], yet there is no negation that does not manifest a phenomenon. However, there are names and expressions that merely negate other phenomena without having a separate referent;
for example, when one says "there is no blue," there is no separate entity of "non-blue" being manifested.

Now, the similarity between the subject and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is intended primarily to assist the reason (*hetu*) in establishing the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣa*). It is said that all things produced (*kṛtaka*) must necessarily be expressed.
Since that which manifests what is produced necessarily excludes [its opposite], it follows that excluding all non-produced things as impermanent must manifest impermanence;
because manifestation necessarily excludes, it excludes permanence. Thus, while the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) manifests, it simultaneously excludes its "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*).
The original purpose of the dissimilar instance was to prevent confusion regarding those who claim permanence; it merely excludes impermanence and does not intend to manifest [permanence].
The statement "it is not produced" merely negates being produced; it does not intend to separately define the essence of what is "not produced.

Therefore, the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) merely negates and does not positively describe. Prior to Dignāga, all masters took the subject-possessor (*dharmin*), such as space, to be the essence of the dissimilar example.
They formulated the syllogism as follows: "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced," with the similar example being [the same].
The positive example (*anvaya*) states, "like a jar," meaning that a jar is impermanent. The negative example (*vyatireka*) states, "not like space," meaning that what is not like space is permanent.
Dignāga refutes this by citing the third formulation: "Sound is produced by diligent and uninterrupted effort, because it possesses the nature of impermanence.
The positive example here is "like a jar," meaning that a jar is produced by diligent...
It is produced by effort. As for the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): "It is not like space; it is not like space because it is not produced by diligent effort.

Furthermore, as stated in the ninth proposition: "Sound is eternal," with the reason being "because it is unobstructed" and the similar example being "like space," the dissimilar example is "not like a jar.
If you were to point to space as the dissimilar example, then these two reasons would necessarily be [identical].
Since the "correct reason" (saddhetu) occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), it becomes an "inconclusive reason" (anaikāntika-hetu).
How then can you claim that its essence consists merely in the existence of the subject (dharmin)? If, as I propose, one were to state the general characteristic simply as:

"Whatever is eternal is not produced, like space," this would exclude reasons that occur in only a portion of the dissimilar instances; for both [the reason and the example] occur within the dissimilar instances.

Therefore, it is not a correct reason (*hetu*). [Question: Why is it that for the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the reason is stated first and the thesis (*pakṣa*) follows later, whereas for the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the thesis is stated first and the absence of the reason follows? Why cannot this order be reversed? [Answer:
When one says, "Because it is a product (*kṛtakatvāt*)," the intended meaning is: "Because it is a product, it is therefore impermanent. This is the method for the similar instance.
Since the example serves to assist this reason in proving the meaning of impermanence, one must first state the "produced nature" (*kṛtakatva*) and subsequently describe "impermanence.

Furthermore, the purpose of the negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is primarily to prevent ambiguity; therefore, one first clarifies its dissimilarity to the thesis (*pakṣa*) and only thereafter demonstrates that the reason does not exist [in the counter-example].
Moreover, it is explained that if one were to reverse this order, the reason of "produced nature" and the reason of "arising from effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) would each incur two fallacies.
Regarding the two faults of the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*): first, the fault of establishing something distinct from the thesis; second, the fault of restating what is already established.

What is meant? If one uses the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) to illustrate the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), saying that "all impermanent things are produced," and then uses the dissimilar instance to illustrate the similar instance, saying that "all non-produced things are permanent," this constitutes a separate [fault].

To establish the thesis that "the produced" (kṛtaka) by means of the reason "impermanence," or to establish the thesis that "the eternal" (nitya) by means of the reason "the unproduced" (akṛtaka), does not prove the fundamental meaning of the thesis of impermanence;
this is the fallacy of establishing a distinct and divergent thesis (*anyathāsiddha*).

Furthermore, since it is already universally established (*prasiddha*) that jars and the like are produced while space and the like are eternal, what cause is there to establish them anew? This is the fallacy of re-establishing what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

[Objection: "If that which is produced (*kṛtaka*) upon the jar is already established as being inherently proven, then this is the fallacy of proving again what has already been established (*siddhasādhana*).
Since both parties already accept that the jar is impermanent, what is the use of the reason 'being produced' to prove it again? [Response: Because the jar is produced, it is impermanent;

by this very proof, one establishes that sound is also impermanent because it is produced. Therefore, the property of being produced in the jar does not need to be separately established as impermanent."
Because the jar is impermanent, its being a product is not used to prove that sound is impermanent simply because it is also a product.

Regarding the two faults of reiterating the nature of being a product as impermanent upon the jar and the exertion of effort [in the reason], they are: first, the fault of establishing a distinct thesis;
second, the fault of establishing what is undesirable. Why? If one uses a similar instance to categorize a dissimilar instance, saying "all things that are... [the following faults ensue].

That which is permanent is all produced by diligent effort; furthermore, using a dissimilar example to illustrate a similar one, [the opponent] claims that whatever is not produced by diligent effort is permanent.

This is to establish the thesis that "that which is produced by diligent effort" by using "impermanence" as the reason, and to establish the thesis of "permanence" by using "not being produced immediately after diligent effort" as the reason—this fails to prove the fundamental point.
The thesis that "all things are inherently impermanent" commits the fallacy of establishing a distinct and contradictory position.
Furthermore, while jars and the like are impermanent and produced through effort, lightning and the like are impermanent yet not produced through effort;
how can you claim they are of the same class by asserting that "all impermanent things are produced through effort"? Moreover, space is not produced through effort, yet it is... [impermanent].

If lightning is not produced through effort yet is impermanent, how can you claim that because they belong to different categories, all things not produced through effort are likewise eternally abiding?
Since both of these reasons exist within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), what you are now establishing is actually the establishment of the very opposite of your own intended thesis:
namely, that the essence of lightning and such things is indeed produced through effort and is eternally abiding.
This would also result in the fault of [the thesis] being undesirable.
Having already explained the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, the commentary states:
"The following constitutes the third section, the definitive conclusion, which has three parts: first, the general conclusion; second, the specific conclusions; and third, the refutation."
This calculation constitutes the summary: it refers to what has already been explained above regarding the names and entities of the "prover" (*sādhana*), such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
When such manifold statements are presented to others for their instruction, they are termed the "prover."

The commentary states: Below this, there are two distinct conclusions: first, the conclusion regarding the name; second, the conclusion regarding the essence. This is the conclusion regarding the name.
For example, the statement "sound is impermanent" is the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The commentary states: From here below, the conclusion (*nigamana*) has four parts: first, the conclusion of the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the conclusion of the reason (*hetu*); third, the conclusion of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*);
and fourth, the conclusion of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). This [section] is the conclusion of the thesis.
"Because of the property of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
The commentary states: This concludes the section on the reason (*hetu*). Regarding "the nature of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), its essence is the property of the reason (*hetudharma*);

as for the term "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*), it is explained by means of the *tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning that it is called the "property of the thesis" because it is a property belonging to the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
"If that which is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a jar and so forth," is the statement "conforming to the similar class" (*sapakṣānugama*). The commentary states:

this concludes the discussion of the similar example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Because the "produced nature" (*kṛtakatva*) present in the jar is the same as the "produced nature" present in sound, it is called the "similar class.

Since the impermanence in the jar conforms to this similar class, it is said to "conform to the similar class"; that is, because the impermanence of the jar conforms [to the property of being produced].
Because it belongs to the same class (*sapakṣa*), it reveals that the impermanence of sound also conforms to the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).
Alternatively, it may be said that the "producedness" inherent in sound conforms to the "producedness" inherent in a jar; therefore, it is called "conforming to the same class."
If it is argued that the "permanent" is unconditioned like space and so forth, this is a statement of exclusion (*vyatireka*).

The commentary states: this concludes the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*); where the probandum (*sādhya*)—the thesis of impermanence—is absent, the probans (*sādhana*)—the reason of being conditioned—is also excluded.
"Only these three parts are called the 'proof' (*sādhana*).
[The commentary] states: This is a refutation of certain views. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is to be established;

it is for the sake of establishing this thesis that only the reason (*hetu*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) are called the "proof. Since it says "only these," it excludes the ancient masters' inclusion of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the application (*upanaya*).
The formulation [of the thesis] is also established as a member of the proof (*sādhana-aṅga*) in order to exclude the "member of investigation" (*parīkṣā-aṅga*) posited by the non-Buddhists.
The ancient masters regarded the thesis (*pakṣa*) as a member of the proof, as has been extensively analyzed above. Now, Dignāga says:
since the thesis is merely a requisite for the proponent (*vādī*), how could it be a member of the proof? It is like the fact that one who is capable of shooting requires only a bow and arrows.
The target at which one shoots is merely an instrument required for the act of shooting; it is not the shooter itself. The ancient masters combined [the arguments] and said:

"Since sound is impermanent, one should know that it is also without self (*anātman*). This is precisely the meaning of the *jāti* (logical class) syllogism, because that which is impermanent must necessarily be without self.
Dignāga stated: "This is what is intended by oneself, and it is stated incidentally to reveal the tenets of the treatise."
If nothing is established in the middle [of the argument], why is it necessary to say that one must further clarify the meaning intended beyond the thesis (*pakṣa*)?
Since this would be far too prolix, I do not venture to provide the members of the proof (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the ancient masters and the Hīnayānists would state together:
"The pot is produced; the pot is impermanent; therefore, one should know that sound is produced and is likewise impermanent. This is what they assert.
Regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one should state: "Whatever is produced is impermanent. This already demonstrates that sound is impermanent;
why then is it necessary to establish a separate member of the syllogism called the application (*upanaya*)? The ancient masters concluded by saying: "Therefore, sound is impermanent. Dignāga stated:
"Since impermanence was originally established and proven sufficient through the three members [of the syllogism], why is it necessary [to state the conclusion]?"
The conclusion states: "Sound is impermanent. If one were not to conclude thus, would it not then be permanent? Therefore, I do not establish a fifth member called the "conclusion" (*nigamana*).
The non-Buddhists say that when establishing a thesis, one must first determine the fundamental position (*pakṣa*) before engaging in debate;

they thus establish the member of "examination" (*parīkṣā*). Dignāga refutes this, stating: "It is because there is the stump [of the tree], and so forth, up to because there is the person who realizes the meaning [of the proof]."
Only then can a formal argument be established; how could all [these elements] possibly be constituent members of the proof (*sādhana*)?

Therefore, it is only through these three members that the meaning of the sound’s impermanence is established. This is the intention of Dignāga: he intends to omit [redundant parts] so as to manifest the meaning directly, rather than employing superfluous words.

Thus, the constituent members of the proof consist of only three. If, at the time of establishing the argument, one were to include the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*), [it would likewise be redundant].
If there is no fault, yet one merely establishes a distinct number of members, this cannot be questioned.

For example, when establishing that form (*rūpa*) is empty because it arises dependently, like a magical illusion—since there is no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), why is it said that the three members constitute the proof?
The answer is: the word "only" used here merely excludes the four [other] members; it does not mean that the proof must necessarily possess these three. Why do you ask this?

If it is argued that the reason "because of dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) does not manifest the thesis because the thesis lacks the three characteristics [of a valid reason], we reply: this is like the case of the reason "because of being a single characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇatvāt*).

Since the example of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is established to exclude the dissimilar class, and since there is no dissimilar class for this reason, the reason does not function erroneously; thus, there is no dissimilar example, and the meaning of the thesis is established.

The previously stated formal inference (*pramāṇa*) suffers from the fallacy of being counterbalanced by a contradictory reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). That is to say, the reason "because of dependent origination" is fixed as follows: [the opponent might argue that] since the reason is fixed, it is contradictory.
The ability to manifest the tenets possesses the first two characteristics because it does not function within the practice of other schools.
Regarding the question of why there are only three means of proof (*sādhana*) and no other established meanings, the answer is that the means of proof consist of only three:

the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) establishes through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), while the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) excludes through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Thus, there is no similarity [to other schools], and the heterodox outsiders (*tīrthika*) are not of this class.
Furthermore, there are instances where only a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is established to refute this position by means of three criteria, as detailed in the *Śata-śāstra*;
these need not be described here at length.
Although one may wish to establish [a thesis], it is termed a "pseudo-thesis" (*pratijñābhāsa*) because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of valid cognition.

The commentary states: From here below begins the second major section, the explanation of fallacious propositions (*pratijñābhāsa*). This section has two parts: first, the individual explanations; second, the summary conclusion. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, the explanation of fallacious propositions; second, the explanation of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*); and third, the explanation of fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

Now, first is the explanation of fallacious propositions, which has three sub-sections: first, a general clarification; second, individual explanations; and third, a definitive conclusion. This [present passage] constitutes the general clarification.
Regarding the meaning established by "desire" (iṣṭa), it encompasses both the real and the pseudo;

although that which is desired constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established, because it contradicts the nine types of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the pseudo is not the real.

That is to say: contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), contradiction with one's own scripture (*āgama*), contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka*), contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana*), the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), the non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddha*), the non-establishment of both, and that which is established by mere conformity (*prasiddhasamjñaka*).
The commentary states: Below this, there is a detailed explanation in three parts: first, listing the names; second, discerning their essential natures; and third, explaining their meanings.
This [section] is the listing of the names.
Among these, "contradiction with direct perception" (*pratyakṣa-viruddha*) refers, for example, to saying that sound is not audible.
The commentary states: Below this, the nine fallacies are distinguished as nine sections. Within each individual fallacy, the chapter is first cited and then the dharma is presented.
This is the first fallacy: there are three types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely, (1) self-perception, (2) other-perception, and (3) common perception.

Alternatively, there may be a thesis that contradicts one's own direct perception, rather than being perceived by another or commonly perceived. For example, as when a Vaiśeṣika proponent establishes a doctrine against a Buddhist, saying:
The real entities of earth, water, and fire are not actually seen by the eye because they differ from blue and other colors; the concordant example is "like fragrance, taste, and so forth.

Since the Vaiśeṣika school’s own tenet asserts that the real entities of earth, water, and fire—which serve as the substrata for color—are also visible, this constitutes a fault of contradicting one's own scriptures (*sva-āgama-virodha*).
However, here we are primarily concerned with the meaning of contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*); the others are listed [elsewhere].
However, there may be cases where a thesis is established that contradicts another's direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but not one's own or both;

this is like the Buddhist establishment of the following inference, which contradicts only another: "There may be a case where a thesis is established that contradicts common direct perception, but not another's or one's own;

for example, as when a Vaiśeṣika master establishes a proposition against a follower of the Buddha, saying: 'Visible form is not seen by the eye, because it is subject to transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma*),' just as..."

Just as with fragrance and so forth, since both the Vaiśeṣika masters and the disciples of the Buddha agree that color-form (*rūpa*) is an object of the senses, if it contradicts what is accepted by both oneself and others, it is subsumed under this fault;
however, if it contradicts only others and not one's own position, it is not categorized as a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).

This contradiction with the other’s valid cognition (*parapramāṇa*)—such as when a person with clear vision says that what is seen by one with cataracts is unreal—is without fault. Now, in this case...
In this passage, only the contradiction with the *sādhāraṇa* (common) [reason] is raised, while the contradiction with the *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon) is omitted.
"Sound" (*śabda*) is the *dharmin* (subject), and "not being audible" (*aśrāvaṇatva*) is the *dharma* (predicate). The combination of the *dharma* and the *dharmin* constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).

To say that sound is not audible contradicts the fact that sound is an object heard by the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), which are forms of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, it constitutes a fault in the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*). This is what is meant by the term "direct perception."
The meaning may be inferred from the explanation below.
Regarding "contradiction with inference" (*anumāna-viruddha*): for example, to say that jars and the like are permanent.

The commentary states: This second fault of inference also includes the categories of self, other, and common [inference], just as when a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) debates against one of the Greater Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).
The established tenet states: "Present phenomena alone possess the power and function to take an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

This thesis contradicts one's own inference (*sva-anumāna*). To contradict one's own inference means that present phenomena necessarily lack the power and function to take an outflowing fruit because they possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*), just like past and future phenomena.
Furthermore, this very tenet contradicts the inference of others (*para-anumāna*).

That which contradicts inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is as follows: "Present phenomena (*dharma*) necessarily lack the power and capacity to grasp a concordant result (*niṣyandaphala*), because they are not substantially existent (*dravyasat*);
just like past and future [phenomena]. This very thesis contradicts common inference (*sāmānyānumāna*). That which contradicts common inference is as follows:
"Present phenomena necessarily lack the power and capacity to grasp a concordant result, because they are included within the world (*loka*); just like..."
To contradict both one's own [tenet] and what is common [to others] is subsumed under the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*); to contradict only the other [party] is not a fault.

Here, we cite only that which contradicts what is common to inference (*sādhāraṇānumāna*). For example, to propose as a thesis that "the subject (*dharmin*), such as a jar, is permanent" with respect to its property (*dharma*)—where the general characteristics of both the property and the subject constitute the thesis—is a contradiction of what is common.
First, there is no [inference to support it], and subsequently, there is no valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That is to say, [it is claimed that] jars and the like are certainly...

Because impermanence has neither beginning nor end, it is like a lamp flame and so forth; one should consider that there are also contradictions with the reason (*viruddha-hetu*) and contradictions with the specific property of the subject (*dharmaviśeṣa-viruddha*), following the same principle.
The meaning of these inferences (*anumāna*) should also be understood according to the explanation provided below.
Regarding contradiction with one's own school (*sva-śāstra-virodha*): for example, the Vaiśeṣika masters establish sound as permanent.
The commentary states: "This third fault, contradiction with one's own school, also has three types—namely, contradiction with oneself, with others, and with both.

For instance, if the Vaiśeṣika masters, whose tenet establishes that sound is subsumed under the category of quality (*guṇa-pada*) and is impermanent in essence, were to posit [the following] against the Śabdanaya (Proponents of Sound): 'Sound...'"
If one constantly contradicts one’s own school by establishing this proposition against the disciples of the Buddha and others, it contradicts the shared teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

If one establishes the impermanence of sound against a proponent of phonology (*śabda-vādin*), it contradicts the other's teaching (*para-śāsana*). This also contradicts both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the shared [teaching], and is thus a fault of the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*);
whereas contradicting the other's teaching is not a fault of the thesis. Question: Is contradicting one’s own school when establishing the thesis [considered a fault]?
Question: Why does citing one’s own scripture to prove a thesis not constitute a valid reason? Answer: This is because it still relies on another;

for instance, if one were to disparage one’s own father and thereby become a wicked person, yet cite that very father to demonstrate one’s own capability, such a person cannot be relied upon or trusted. Thus, to contradict one’s own scripture is a fault, and citing one’s own scripture does not serve as proof.
Contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka-viruddha*) is, for example, as when it is said that the hare-marked [moon] is not the moon because it does not exist [as such],
or as when it is said that human skull-bone is pure because it is a part of a sentient being, just like a conch shell.
The commentary states: This fourth fault concerns two types of "worldly" (loka): first, the world of those in training (*śaikṣa*), and second, the world of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
One is designated as "in training" by virtue of their practice, while one is designated as "beyond training" not by virtue of practice.

Because each is commonly recognized by many people, they are called "worldly. There are three types of the world of those in training: first, those who are like oneself, such as the disciples of the Buddha.

1. From the perspective of one's own school, [the thesis] "the self does not exist" and so forth is [a case of] contradicting oneself, as in the case of a Buddhist disciple regarding the followers of Ulūka (Vaiśeṣika). 2.

From the perspective of another, such as a Buddhist disciple regarding the followers of Ulūka, it is [a case of] contradicting another, as in the case of the "self" and so forth practiced by them. 3. Commonly, as when a Buddhist disciple and the followers of Ulūka look at each other, it is [a case of] contradicting both, as they both practice that coarse matter is impermanent and so forth;
if one establishes a thesis that contradicts one's own position, such as a Buddhist disciple establishing that "the self exists."

This refers only to what is expected from one's own school; thus, it is called "contradicting one's own teaching" (*sva-śāstra-virodha*) and "contradicting worldly meaning" (*loka-artha-virodha*). It does not mean contradicting the world in general.
For instance, when a Buddhist disciple establishes a thesis such as "there is no self" against a follower of Ulūka, this is not a fault, because the purpose of a treatise is to refute others.
However, if the thesis established contradicts what is commonly accepted—as is the case with Buddhist disciples and others—[it constitutes a fault].
To establish that coarse matter is permanent and so forth is subsumed under the fault of contradicting worldly consensus (*loka-viruddha*).
"The world of non-learners" refers to those such as cowherds who all commonly understand that there is the nature of form and so forth.

If one follows popular sentiment and establishes the substantial nature of the eye, form, and so forth according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet asserts that their essence is empty, this contradicts common worldly understanding and is therefore subsumed under the fault of the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*).
If one establishes a thesis by distinguishing it according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), although it may contradict worldly sentiment, it is not a fault of the thesis;

for the ultimate truth is not known through conventional cognition. In this present text, we cite only that which contradicts what is not learned by the world—such as the notion that the hare-marked [moon] is a person or that a human skull is impure—because these are not understood through study and training. If someone were to establish [a position] such as:
The proposition that "the hare-marked [moon] is not the moon" takes "because it possesses [a mark]" as the reason and "like the sun" as the example.
Furthermore, the Śikhin heretics, who pierce human skulls with strings to adorn their bodies and claim them to be pure, formulate the following argument:

they take "human skulls are pure" as the proposition (*pakṣa*), "because they are parts of sentient beings" as the reason (*hetu*), and "like conch shells" as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). These are the two types of formulated propositions.
Although phenomena (*dharma*) and their substrata (*dharmī*) are not mutually separable, this [position] is a fault because it contradicts worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*).

This is because people of the world universally designate the moon as "the one who embraces the hare" (*śaśin*) and describe the cranial bone as "impure. Question: What is the difference between this and contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
Answer: One should formulate four logical possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*): there may be that which contradicts the world but does not contradict direct perception; this is precisely that case.
The thesis that "the hare-marked [moon] is not the moon" and so forth merely contradicts conventional designations commonly transmitted in the world; it does not constitute a logical refutation.

To claim it is "not the moon" does not contradict the fact of visual perception, nor does it contradict direct valid cognition (*pratyakṣa*), just as saying that the five sense organs, such as the eye, are not objects of the *ālayavijñāna* does not contradict worldly convention—because ordinary people do not know that there exists a distinct *ālayavijñāna*.

Therefore, there may be cases where both [criteria] are violated, such as when one says, "Sound is not audible," because it violates the sense that sound is perceived by the ear and so forth, and furthermore, because it violates what is commonly known in the world that sound is audible.
Alternatively, there may be cases where neither is violated; this is not subject to either of the two faults. Question:

If violating direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) necessarily constitutes violating what is commonly known in the world, why is it necessary to mention both? Answer: Because they can be violated separately; violating one does not necessarily entail violating the other.
Therefore, two [types of contradictions] are distinguished.
Regarding "contradiction with one's own words," it is as when one says, "My mother is a barren woman.

The commentary states: this fifth fault, according to the correct translation from the Sanskrit original, should be called "a non-giving woman" (*vṛthā-strī*), meaning a woman who does not produce children.

Since the merit of this [argument] is falsely tainted by the designation "woman," it is called "false woman. Thus, the name remains "false woman" without changing its original translation, which is rendered as "stone-woman" (*śilā-strī*).
My mother is a *dharmin* (subject), and the "stone-woman" is a *dharma* (predicate). The combination of the *dharmin* and the *dharma* constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).
However, the term "*dharmin*" contradicts its own *dharma*, and the term "*dharma*" in turn contradicts the *dharmin*. If one says "my mother," then she is known [to exist].

Since it is not false, stating that "the barren woman" clearly indicates she is not one's mother; because these two statements are mutually contradictory, they are termed "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

Furthermore, when non-Buddhists establish the thesis that "all speech is false," this very statement establishing the thesis is intended by them to be included within the category of "false speech. If one says "all speech," [it immediately includes itself].
If you admit that one portion [of speech] is not false, how can you say that all [speech] is false?

If you say that all [speech] is false, how can you say that "all discourse" [is meant]? This is because the meaning of our own thesis—that which is subsumed under the term "all"—is admitted by us to be non-false.
If they attempt to defend themselves by saying, "Except for my own words, all other words are entirely false," then...
Suppose there is a person who, upon hearing what you have said, declares: "Your words are not false; they are true. Now, would that which he has spoken be false or true?
If you say it is a false statement, then your own words are void. If you say it is true, then it contradicts your own previous assertion.
Furthermore, if you attempt to defend yourself by saying: "Except for my own words and the statement that my words are true, all other words are false," [then...]
If that were so, it would contradict inference (*anumāna*), namely: "All other speech is not necessarily false, because it has the nature of speech," just as you have stated.

As for the case where the differentiator (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not established for the opponent, it is like a Buddhist disciple establishing the destruction of sound (*śabda-nirodha*) against a Sāṃkhya teacher.

The commentary states: This sixth school is the Saṃkhya, which in Chinese is translated as "Number-Theory" (Shùlùn). Because wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to enumerate and measure all phenomena, it is called "Number" (*saṃkhyā*);
because the theory arises from this enumeration, it is called "Number-Theory. The theory can also produce enumeration, and thus it is likewise named "Number-Theory.
The founder of the Number-Theory school is Kapila, which means "Yellow" in Chinese; he was so designated because his head and face were yellow, and he is thus known by that name in the world.
The "Yellow Immortal" (Huang Xianren) is also [referred to as] Kapila; the older transcription "Jiapi luó" is erroneous. This master extensively posits twenty-five principles (*tattva*):

namely, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Great One (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the five organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the mind-organ (*manas*).
Among these, there are four that are unevolved (*avyakta*); that which is not transformed is primordial nature itself, which is capable of producing the Great One and the subsequent principles.

1. Neither derived nor transformative: the *puruṣa* (the principle of the self), because it does not arise from another and does not give rise to others. 2. Transformative but not derived: the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) and the eleven faculties (*indriya*), because they arise solely from another and do not give rise to others.
3. Both derived and transformative: the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the great ego-consciousness (*mahāhaṃkāra*), because these arise from another and also give rise to others.
4. Neither derived nor transformative: the *puruṣa* (the principle of the self), because it does not arise from another and does not give rise to others.
Briefly summarized, these are threefold: self-nature (*svabhāva*), which is the first truth; transformation (*pariṇāma*), which consists of the twenty-three intermediate truths;
and the divine self (*puruṣa*), which is the final truth. Sound is subsumed within the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

Because it originates remotely from self-nature and subsequently transforms back into self-nature, it is called "impermanent" (*anitya*); yet, in its essential nature (*tattva*), it is eternally indestructible.

Now, when a Buddhist disciple establishes against this philosopher the thesis that "sound is perishable" (śabdo vināśī), where "perishability" is the property to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*) and "sound" is the subject to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*), this is commonly accepted.
However, for the Sāṃkhya, the property of "perishability" as the distinguisher (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not established, because in the Sāṃkhya school there is no such phenomenon as perishability.

Therefore, this is merely a case of the non-establishment of the distinguisher for the other [party]. If a Buddhist disciple were to establish against a Sāṃkhya philosopher the thesis that "the eye must necessarily..."
If the Puruṣa’s experience of hearing this [sound] is taken as the probans (*sādhana*), it constitutes the fallacy of the unestablished specific property (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇāsiddha*).

If one were to posit the substance of sound (*śabda-tattva*) as the substratum (*āśraya*) for both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) in order to establish this against the Sāṃkhya school, it would constitute the fallacy of the unestablished common specific property (*asiddha-sādhāraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*).
Because these are omitted in the text, only the other [fallacy] is mentioned.
Regarding the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*): for example, when a Sāṃkhya teacher proposes to a Buddhist disciple that "the self (*ātman*) is volition.
The commentary states: This seventh fault—asking why this unestablished locus is not subsumed under the category of the thesis (*pakṣa*) because it lacks a substratum—is answered as follows:
The unestablished locus is definitely a fault of the thesis, because it is included within the nine types of fallacies.

It is just as in the other eight [schools], or as in the other five Sāṃkhya masters’ tenets, which hold that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are merely discerning wisdom (*buddhi*), while volition (*cetanā*) belongs exclusively to the function of the *puruṣa* (the self). Therefore, in establishing their doctrinal position in opposition to the Buddha-dharma, they state:
"The *puruṣa* is the agent of volition; the self is a substantial entity (*dharmin*), and volition is its attribute (*dharma*). Furthermore, volition is the differentiator."

Both schools agree that "I" is the object to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*), yet because the Buddha's teachings do not tolerate it, this "object to be distinguished" is not established for both parties (*aprasiddha*).
Question: If one qualifies the thesis with the term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*), there is no fault of contradicting worldly convention;

now, if one qualifies the "object to be distinguished" with the phrase "as admitted by oneself," can it be established? Answer: When both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are established, one may indeed qualify [the object] with "ultimate reality."

The "refutation of the fault through the meaning" (*arthasamkṣepa*) means that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the essence of the eyes and so forth is empty. As for the "self" (*ātman*) which is distinguished [from them], it is commonly accepted by both [parties];
even if one were to say "it is accepted by oneself," it would ultimately not be established for the other. Therefore, this is not a valid analogy.

This phrase "accepted by oneself" merely excludes common inference (*sādhāraṇānumāna*) to demonstrate that one's own inference (*svatantrānumāna*) is free from the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*). This is precisely what constitutes the "unestablished nature of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) for the other party.
The fact that both [the self and the atoms] are not ultimate atoms can be understood by reflecting on the categories subsumed within this [section],
such as when the Vaiśeṣika masters establish the self (*ātman*) as the cause of conjunction.
The commentary states: This eighth school is the Vaiśeṣika, which is translated here as "Victorious" (Śe-shi).
Its treatise extensively expounds the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) through the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), and as it is rarely equaled by other treatises, it is called "Victorious.
The older transliterations "Vaiśeṣika" or "Vaiśeṣika" are all corruptions. The author of this treatise is named Ulūka, whose full account will be related below.
In this Vaiśeṣika school, there are six categories (*padārtha*): the self (*ātman*) is the first category, and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the sixth.
When various phenomena aggregate together, the nature of conjunction arises; however, the arising of this nature of conjunction depends upon the self as its condition.

Regarding this, they establish this doctrine in opposition to the Buddha’s teachings, claiming that the self is the causal condition for conjunction and that the self is an existing entity that constitutes the basis for conjunction.

Regarding the combination of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), since this school of Buddhist doctrine does not admit a "self" (*ātman*) and there is no such thing as "combination," both [theories] fail individually.
Question: In this context, do you take "causes and conditions" as the basis for grasping, or do you take "combination"?
If so, what is the fault? If you take causes and conditions, that is already fully established, as it is admitted by the Buddhist doctrine. If you take combination...

If they are combined, they cannot be the distinguisher because they possess distinct natures. In response: since this [argument] uses "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) to designate the causes and conditions, those causes and conditions themselves are also not established.
This too is merely a case where both parties fail to establish their position; whether from one's own perspective or from a common perspective, it is subsumed under this same fault.
This can be understood by applying the analogy accordingly.
"Consistent with what is universally established" (*prasiddha-samāna*) refers, for example, to saying that sound is audible.
[The commentary] states: This is the ninth fault. Now, the purpose of formulating a treatise is to refute erroneous doctrines and to dismantle opposing schools.

Since the audibility of sound is admitted by both the proponent and the opponent, and since this point of observation is already identical, how could it require verbal proof? Therefore, this constitutes a formal thesis (*pakṣa*).
Question: Since the Lord of Devas (Dignāga) has already established the [first] four fallacies, why did Dharmakīrti establish the latter four fallacies separately?
Answer: This is based on a distinction in meaning, and there is no contradiction in principle.

As for Dharmakīrti not establishing the fallacy of "unestablished qualification" (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), it is because this is already included within the fallacy of "unestablished thesis" (*asiddha*) among the pseudo-reasons and pseudo-examples. That is to say, according to the Sāṃkhya school...
The nature of the self (*ātman*) is eternal, whereas all else merely undergoes transformation without being subject to total destruction. Now, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established as follows:
"Sound is subject to destruction because it is produced. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) states: "Whatever is produced is entirely subject to destruction, such as a lamp-flame.
Upon that lamp-flame, there exists only the probans (*sādhana*), namely the reason of being produced, which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*).

The Sāṃkhya school neither accepts nor establishes the destruction [of the self]. Furthermore, regarding the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*)—since the substratum for this reason is not established—the treatise states the thesis:
"The divine self exists. It provides the reason: "Because it is the substratum of qualities.
Since this reason, "the substratum of qualities," lacks a substratum, it constitutes a logical fallacy. If the self is originally non-existent, yet one now establishes it...
Because [the reason] exists, there is no fault in the thesis; its non-establishment in both cases is entirely identical to these two [previous faults].

Furthermore, that which is not established as a "concordant with what is already established" (prasiddha-sapakṣa) is as follows: since the thesis to be established involves mutual contradiction—such as "sound is audible," which is originally and universally accepted and thus inherently not a [novel] thesis—it is impossible to discuss a fault therein.
Therefore, among the faults of a thesis, these four types do not exist. However, the Lord of Heaven (Devanampriya)...

Because it is presented with full logical reasoning, the four types of fallacies are added; although the "unestablishedness of the predicate" (*asiddha-pakṣadharma*) is indeed a fallacy similar to that found in the pseudo-example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), why should it not also be a fallacy within the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself?

If one were to argue that the Sāṃkhya school does not accept destruction, and therefore establishing destruction is precisely what constitutes the thesis and thus is not a fallacy of the thesis—this argument fails because there is no similar example (*sapakṣa*).
Ultimately, there is no fault in establishing "presently" as an additional category of *pakṣābhāsa* (fallacies of the thesis). If it is argued:

"Since this is already a fallacy within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), why must it be established separately as a fallacy of the thesis?"—the answer is that since the thesis (*pakṣa*) takes the nature of inseparability (*avinābhāva*) as its object, and since there is nothing that can differentiate [the subject], how could that which is not separated [from the subject] not be established?
Thus, the differentiator (*viśeṣaṇa*) fails to be established as the thesis; although the differentiated (*viśeṣya*) is not established, it remains the locus (*āśraya*).
If [the fault of] non-establishment is not abandoned, why is it not also a fault within the thesis (*pakṣa*)?

If you say that this is a fault of the reason (*hetu*) and there is no need to establish it separately as a fault of the thesis, then since both the property of the thesis and the property of the reason equally lack a basis, why is one a fault while the other is not?
If you say that our Buddhist doctrine does not permit me to establish "self" (*ātman*), and that the correct and conforming thesis is inseparable [from the reason], [then the fault remains].

If the nature [of the thesis] has already been established as the very point of the thesis (*siddhānta*), there can be nothing further to be distinguished. Since there is nothing to be distinguished, the "thing to be distinguished" is not established; this is a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).

If both [the reason and the example] are likewise unestablished, they are identical to these two aforementioned faults. If one establishes a thesis in order to refute another's position, yet that thesis accords with what the other has established, it is subsumed under these faults.
If one argues that because it accords with what was originally established, it is not a thesis and thus cannot be called a fault—[this is not so]. Both...

Since neither [position] establishes its own thesis and neither is a valid reason—because it is not a reason—it constitutes a fault in the argument; thus, O Lord of Devas, there are nine faults in your school's position.
Such manifold statements are for the purpose of negating the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

The commentary states: Below this is the third section, the explanation of the meaning, which has three parts: first, the explanation of the initial five faults; second, the explanation of the middle three faults;
and third, the explanation of the final one fault. This [section] explains the aforementioned five faults. Since it cites the previous nine faults, it says:
"Thus, regarding these many words, why do they contradict those five, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? These five are faults of the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*). This is because of these five...
The "principle" (mūla) here refers to the gate of negating the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. This is because sound is the specific characteristic of all phenomena;

this specific characteristic of sound is that which is heard by the ear and so forth, and it serves as the gateway for the universal production of auditory consciousness. Thus, the object that is heard is designated as the "gate.

Now, when it is said that "sound is not what is heard," one does not lose the specific characteristic of sound itself; rather, one merely negates the gate of "being heard. Therefore, [the specific characteristic of sound remains].
The fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*) has been explained; the remaining four types of fallacies can be understood by analogy with this.

Since they cannot be established [as valid], it is said: "In this explanation, why are these three—namely, the unestablished nature of the subject (*pakṣa-asiddhi*) and so forth—considered fallacies?"

Because it cannot be established, the thesis (*pakṣa*) cannot stand; for the essential point of establishing a thesis is that it must encompass phenomena such that the phenomena so encompassed can be established, yet the opposing position (*pratipakṣa*) cannot be admitted.
Since the meaning of the thesis thus lacks any basis of support, these three types constitute faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).
"Because establishing [the thesis] would be fruitless.
The commentary states: This explains the final fault. Why is this considered a fault? It is because establishing [the thesis] would be fruitless.

Now, one who establishes a thesis does so to eliminate prior doubts and give rise to new understanding; yet, regarding the object heard by the auditory consciousness, all [cognizers] already possess recognition.
To know that restating this [proposition] before an assembly is fruitless and of no benefit is the fault;
it is called the "fault resembling the failure to establish a thesis.
The commentary states: "This is the third [point], which establishes the conclusion."
Having already explained the fallacies of the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) shall now be explained.

The commentary states: "From here below is the second [section], the explanation of the fallacies of the reason, which has two parts: first, concluding the previous section and promising the explanation; second, the actual analysis of the fallacies of the reason.
This [paragraph] constitutes the first part.
That which is unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or contradictory (*viruddha*) is called a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
The commentary states: from here below, the fallacious reasons are correctly analyzed in two parts: first, a general clarification; second, a detailed explanation. This is the first part.

A reason possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) alone can establish the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣa*); if one does not properly understand the first characteristic, there is the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
If one does not properly understand that the latter two characteristics involve the fallacy of being indeterminate or contradictory,
why are they called "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth? If the reason proposed is not admitted by both parties regarding the thesis, or is not admitted by either one,
or is subject to doubt, or lacks a locus for the thesis— such a reason is called "unestablished," just like the thesis itself.
If one claims that when both [the reason and the thesis] fail to be established, this constitutes "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by way of the nature of the reason itself, that is not so.
For instance, although the reason "the nature of being audible" cannot establish the thesis, it is not subsumed under the four types of unestablished reasons.
How, then, can one say it is "unestablished" simply because it does not establish the thesis? If...

If the reason established is such that it exists in the similar instances and does not exist in the dissimilar instances, or if it does not exist in both the similar and dissimilar instances, or even if it exists in the similar instances but does not exist in the dissimilar instances, it contradicts the opponent’s own measure (*pramāṇa*).
Since its nature is thus not determined according to one's own desired tenet, it is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, if the reason established does not exist in the similar instances but exists in the dissimilar instances, or if it exists in the similar instances but does not exist in the dissimilar instances, it still contradicts what is accepted by one's own school.
Because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established as intended, it is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*). There are four types of non-establishment (*asiddha*). The commentary states:

what follows is a detailed explanation in three parts: first, the explanation of non-establishment; second, the explanation of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); and third, the explanation of the contradictory (*viruddha*).
Regarding the three types of non-establishment due to contradiction: first, stating the number; second, listing the names; third, explaining their essential natures. This [section] states the number:

Or is it indeed the color of consciousness, because—just as our own school admits—the forms of Buddhas in other realms are included within the first three elements yet are not apprehended by the eye?

If one does not state "admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*), then one cannot raise the objection of an "inconclusive fallacy" (*anaikāntika*) against another, nor can one pose the challenge of a "contradiction" (*viruddha*).
However, if one simply states that [the subject] is included in the first three [categories] while not being included by the eye, one can still raise the inconclusive fallacy;

why then is it necessary to say "admitted by oneself"? Answer: If one does not say "admitted by oneself," then there would be an inconclusive fallacy for the other party. That is to say, the other party would commit an inconclusive fallacy. This is because the other party would be making [an argument] that is not...

Regarding the objection concerning the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): Is it like the case where color established by common consensus (*prasiddha*), though included within the first three [elements] of the eye-consciousness and not included by the eye itself, is not necessarily separated from the eye-consciousness?

Or is it like our own school’s position that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, while actually possessing unwholesome color included within the first three [elements] of the eye-consciousness and not included by the eye itself, is necessarily separated from the eye-consciousness? To avoid this fault, it says "by oneself" (*sva*).

If one were to avoid this fault by stating "that which is admitted [by us] and is included within the first three [elements], but not included by the eye," then it would be impossible to formulate a counter-objection (*prasaṅga*) against the opponent that would result in an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason;
therefore, the term "admitted by oneself" (*sva-siddha*) alone is used.
*Commentary on the Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, Scroll One.

In the spring of the tenth year of Kōsei (1798), the year of Wuwu, the master Tan’ei of the Zekishin-in in Rakyō lectured on the Great Commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa* at the Tenjinsha Shrine in Sakai, Izumi Province. That temple is the former site of Gokushū.
The Master of Calligraphy (Yingshi) examined the catalog of books held by Juezhou and found that it included three fascicles of the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra-vṛtti*.
He subsequently sought them out, but the temple master had only obtained the first fascicle;
the remaining two fascicles were missing from Juezhou’s inventory (and so forth). In the past, while I was examining the *Nyāyapraveśaka*, I encountered this new commentary.

Because the treatises of many [scholars] deviated from the principles of the *Nyāyamukha* and I could not find ancient commentaries to resolve this, I have used reason to extend the orthodox tradition of *Hetuvidyā*, refuting their heterodox records and documenting it in three volumes of the *Hetuvidyā-saṃkṣepa-viniścaya-ṭīkā* and three volumes of the *Gungong*.
This year, fortunately, I heard that there was a commentary on the *Wengu* (Textual Principles); I have earnestly requested the original manuscript.
